entry.title: Valencia: City of Light, Paella, and Futuristic Dreams
entry.content:
Valencia sits on Spain's Mediterranean coast in a state of relaxed self-confidence. It is not Madrid's political intensity nor Barcelona's restless exhibitionism — it is a city that has been getting on with things for two thousand years and has the layers to prove it. A Roman forum under a shopping street. A Gothic silk exchange that could pass for a cathedral. A cathedral that may or may not contain the Holy Grail. And then, along the old riverbed that was diverted in 1957 after a catastrophic flood, one of the most audacious urban design projects of the twentieth century: the City of Arts and Sciences, a complex of titanium and concrete so alien-looking that it stops first-time visitors in their tracks.

The City of Arts and Sciences

The Ciutat de les Arts i les Ciències is the project that put modern Valencia on the global architectural map. Designed primarily by Santiago Calatrava (with Félix Candela contributing the L'Umbracle and L'Hemisfèric), the complex stretches for nearly two kilometres along the former Turia riverbed. The L'Hemisfèric, shaped like a giant eye, houses an IMAX cinema and planetarium. The Museu de les Ciències Príncep Felip looks like the skeleton of a prehistoric whale. The L'Oceanogràfic — Europe's largest aquarium — was designed by Félix Candela as a series of hyperbolic paraboloid shells resembling waterlily leaves. Come at dusk when the buildings reflect in the long pools and the light turns everything gold.

The Old City and La Catedral

The old city centres on the Plaza de la Virgen, a baroque square that has served as Valencia's civic heart since Roman times. The Catedral de Valencia is a study in accumulated centuries — Romanesque, Gothic, Renaissance, and Baroque elements layered over the original mosque. Inside, a small agate chalice in the Chapel of the Holy Grail is claimed by some scholars to be the actual cup used at the Last Supper. Whether or not you accept that claim, the Torre del Micalet bell tower offers the finest panorama over the old city's terracotta roofscape.

Two blocks away, the Llotja de la Seda — the Silk Exchange — is one of Spain's finest Gothic buildings and a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Its Sala de Contratació, with twenty-four twisted stone columns rising to a vaulted ceiling, was built in the fifteenth century when Valencia was the wealthiest city in the Iberian Peninsula.

Paella and the Valencian Table

Valencia is where paella was born, and Valencians are unapologetically particular about it. Authentic paella valenciana contains chicken, rabbit, flat green beans, butter beans, saffron, and short-grain rice cooked in a wide, shallow pan over orange wood — and emphatically does not contain seafood (that would be paella de marisco, a different dish). The best place to eat it is along the Malvarrosa beach promenade on a Sunday, where dozens of restaurants serve it to a clientele of local families for whom this is weekly ritual.

The Mercado Central — Valencia's central market, housed in a magnificent Art Nouveau building with a ceramic-tiled dome — is one of the great food markets of Europe. Over a thousand stalls sell the produce of the Valencian huerta: the intensely irrigated market garden that surrounds the city and has been feeding it since Moorish times.

Gotchas & Tips

  • The Turia Gardens: The old Turia riverbed is now a nine-kilometre park running through the heart of the city. Rent a bike and ride the entire length — from the City of Arts and Sciences to the Bioparc — for the best possible introduction to Valencia's geography.
  • Timing Paella: Paella is strictly a lunchtime dish in Valencia. Ordering it for dinner in a serious restaurant will earn you a polite but firm refusal (or a reheated version). Sunday lunch is the canonical moment.
  • Las Fallas: If you visit in mid-March, the city ignites for the Fallas festival — enormous satirical sculptures are paraded through neighbourhoods and then ceremonially burned on the final night. Book accommodation months in advance.
  • Metro vs. Walking: The old city is compact and best on foot. The metro connects the centre to the beach, the airport, and the City of Arts and Sciences efficiently.

Highlights

  • City of Arts and Sciences at Dusk: The golden-hour reflections in the pools are among the most photogenic scenes in contemporary European architecture.
  • Llotja de la Seda: Quiet, spectacular Gothic grandeur with almost none of the crowds that descend on comparable monuments in Seville or Toledo.
  • Mercado Central: Arrive at 10 AM on a weekday for the market at its most alive and the best chance of a conversation with the vendors.
  • Malvarrosa Beach: A proper urban beach, fifteen minutes from the old city by metro, with good waves and a long promenade lined with paella restaurants.

Valencia rewards slow travel. The more time you give it, the more it gives back.

Photo by Matthew Ye on Unsplash

entry.title: Seoul: Where Ancient Palaces Meet Neon Futures
entry.content:
Seoul moves at a speed that other cities aspire to. The transit system is immaculate and frequent, the convenience stores are open all night and genuinely convenient, the food culture is innovative and deeply traditional simultaneously, and the city's relationship with its own past — five royal palaces from the Joseon dynasty intact within the metropolitan area — is one of the most graceful urban negotiations between old and new anywhere in Asia. Seoul is the city that proves you do not have to choose between heritage and ambition.

Gyeongbokgung Palace and Bukchon

Gyeongbokgung Palace — the main royal palace of the Joseon dynasty — was first built in 1395 and is surrounded by over three hundred reconstructed traditional buildings on a site that originally held five hundred. The changing of the guard ceremony at the main gate (10 AM and 2 PM daily) is performed with a precision and colour that rewards attention. Immediately north, the Bukchon Hanok Village is a residential neighbourhood of preserved traditional Korean houses (hanok) on a hillside between the two great palaces — narrow lanes, wooden eaves, stone walls, and the best coffee shops in the city occupying converted hanok interiors.

Hongdae and the Han River

Hongdae — the neighbourhood around Hongik University — is where Seoul's youth culture runs at its most concentrated: indie music venues, street dancers, independent fashion designers, and street food stalls open until 4 AM. The contrast with the palace district thirty minutes away by metro is absolute and is precisely the point about Seoul. The Han River that bisects the city is something that most visitors underuse — the river parks (Yeouido, Banpo) fill with Seoulites cycling, having picnics, and watching the Banpo Bridge Rainbow Fountain (the world's longest bridge fountain) every evening. Joining them is one of the best ways to understand the city.

Gotchas & Tips

  • T-money Card: The transit card that works on metro, bus, and taxis is a non-negotiable Seoul tool — available at any convenience store (GS25, CU, 7-Eleven) for a small deposit, top-up-able anywhere, and giving slightly cheaper fares than paying cash.
  • The Jjimjilbang Experience: A jjimjilbang (Korean public bathhouse) is the essential Seoul experience that most tourists miss. You pay entry (around 10,000–15,000 won), get a uniform, and access saunas at different temperatures, common rooms, and sleeping areas. Many are open 24 hours. It is extraordinary and entirely accessible to non-Korean speakers.
  • Korean BBQ Protocol: At a samgyeopsal (pork belly BBQ) restaurant, the grill is at your table, the side dishes (banchan) are communal and refillable, and the soju or makgeolli is essential. Order the perilla leaf wraps and the doenjang jjigae alongside.

Highlights

  • Namsan Tower and Seoul City Wall: The hike up to N Seoul Tower through the remaining section of the 600-year-old city wall is a meditative experience in the middle of a megacity.
  • Gwangjang Market: Seoul's oldest market, with raw silk, vintage fabric, and a legendary food court where the bindaetteok (mung bean pancakes) and mayak kimbap (sesame rice rolls) are the defining snacks.
  • DMZ Day Trip: The Demilitarised Zone on the North Korean border, reachable on a guided tour from Seoul in two hours, is one of the most historically charged landscapes on earth.
  • Insadong: The traditional arts district, with galleries, tea houses, and the best traditional craft shops in the city — buy a hanji paper product, a celadon teacup, or a handmade ink stick.

Seoul is a city that surprises on every visit. The layers keep revealing themselves, and the depth keeps increasing the more time you give it.

Photo by Markus Winkler on Unsplash

entry.title: Maldives: Overwater Paradise at the Edge of the World
entry.content:
The first time you look down from an overwater bungalow into water so clear that the coral twenty metres below is perfectly visible — and a sea turtle moves through it with absolute unhurried elegance — something recalibrates. The Maldives is one of those places where the natural reality genuinely exceeds what the photographs suggested was possible. The water is the colour that other oceans are trying to be. The reefs are alive in a way that recalibrates your understanding of the word alive. And the stillness here is an active thing — not the absence of noise but the presence of the ocean.

The Overwater Bungalow Experience

The overwater bungalow is the defining architecture of the Maldives — a structure built over the lagoon on wooden stilts, with a glass floor panel above the reef below and a ladder descending directly into the water. Every resort in the Maldives has them in some variation, ranging from simple and affordable to the kind of lavishness that comes with its own plunge pool and butler service. The key variable is the reef directly below: some resorts have live, colourful coral beneath their bungalows; others, degraded or bleached reef. Research the specific reef condition before booking — it makes an enormous difference to the experience of snorkelling from your deck at dawn.

The Reef and What Lives In It

The Maldives sits atop an underwater mountain range — the atolls are the tips of ancient volcanoes — and the nutrient-rich currents that move between the atolls support extraordinary marine biodiversity. Whale sharks — the largest fish on earth — are reliably seen in South Ari Atoll from June to November. Manta rays congregate at cleaning stations across the atolls, hovering while small fish remove parasites in a symbiotic ballet. The house reef of a good resort will offer, on any given morning snorkel, more reef fish species than most people have seen in a lifetime.

Gotchas & Tips

  • The Budget Reality: The Maldives is expensive at the resort level because every resort is its own island — supply chains are complex and there is no local village economy to draw on. The alternative is the local island network — staying in guesthouses on inhabited islands like Maafushi or Ukulhas gives a very different, far more affordable, and genuinely authentic experience of Maldivian daily life.
  • Transfer Logistics: Most resorts are reached by seaplane (spectacular, and the first fifteen minutes of any Maldives trip) or speedboat from Malé. Seaplanes only operate in daylight — if your arrival flight lands after dark, you will overnight in Malé regardless of what the resort website implies.
  • Reef Respect: The Maldives coral reef ecosystem is under serious climate pressure. Snorkel and dive responsibly: no touching, no standing on coral, no sunscreen (use reef-safe mineral-based SPF only), no feeding of fish.

Highlights

  • Dawn Snorkel from Your Deck: Before other guests are awake, the reef below the bungalow belongs entirely to you — the light at this hour through the water is extraordinary.
  • Dhoni Sunset Cruise: A traditional wooden Maldivian sailing boat (dhoni) at sunset, with the atolls spreading to the horizon — this is the correct way to end any day here.
  • Night Snorkel: Many resorts offer night snorkelling with torches — bioluminescent plankton, sleeping parrotfish in their mucous sleeping bags, and moray eels moving freely are all visible.
  • Mas Huni Breakfast: The traditional Maldivian breakfast of smoked tuna, grated coconut, chilli, and onion with flatbread roshi is available on the local islands and at some resorts — extraordinary in simplicity.

The Maldives does not ask you to be anywhere else. For however long you stay, here is entirely sufficient.

Photo by Ishan @seefromthesky on Unsplash

entry.title: Prague: The Fairy-Tale City
entry.content:
There is a moment on Charles Bridge at dawn — before the crowds, before the tour groups, when the morning mist is still threading between the baroque statues and the Vltava River below is perfectly still — when Prague looks less like a city and more like a set designed by someone who wanted to demonstrate what Central European history looked like at its most concentrated and beautiful. It is a city of spires and cobblestones and beer cellars and Kafka, and somehow it holds all of these things without contradiction.

Prague Castle and the Old Town

Prague Castle is the largest ancient castle complex in the world — a hilltop city unto itself, containing a cathedral, royal palace, galleries, gardens, and a golden lane of former alchemists' workshops. St. Vitus Cathedral within the castle complex is Gothic of the highest order, its stained glass by Alfons Mucha among the finest in Europe. From the castle walls, the panorama over the city's red-roofed old town and the river bridges is the quintessential Prague image. Below, the Old Town Square with its astronomical clock (Orloj) and the twin spires of Týn Church is the medieval civic heart — full of crowds but genuinely magnificent even so.

Josefov and the Jewish Quarter

The Jewish Quarter of Josefov contains six historic synagogues and Europe's second-oldest Jewish cemetery — thousands of gravestones stacked in layers, the inscriptions worn by centuries of weather, in a space too small for the number of people buried there. The Old-New Synagogue, dating from 1270, is one of the oldest active synagogues in Europe and contains in its attic, according to legend, the Golem created by Rabbi Loew — a constructed being of clay who protected the Jewish community. This layer of history, legend, and genuine tragedy makes Josefov one of the most affecting districts in any European city.

Gotchas & Tips

  • Charles Bridge Timing: Visit Charles Bridge at dawn or after 9 PM to experience it without crowds. At any other time, the bridge is a slowly moving mass of tourists. The statues — thirty baroque figures added between 1683 and 1714 — are extraordinary; touch the plaque of St. John of Nepomuk (gleaming from millions of hands) for luck.
  • The Beer Reality: Czech beer — specifically Pilsner Urquell and the various Bohemian lager styles — is genuinely extraordinary and remarkably inexpensive. The Lokál restaurant chain serves tank-unpasteurised Pilsner Urquell at the correct temperature and pressure and does a complete Czech menu alongside.
  • Beyond the Old Town: Prague rewards walking away from the tourist centre. The neighbourhoods of Vinohrady (Art Nouveau apartment blocks, independent wine bars) and Žižkov (bohemian, beer-dense, the enormous television tower with baby sculptures) are where contemporary Prague lives.

Highlights

  • St. Vitus Cathedral Stained Glass: Alfons Mucha's nave window glows with colour in a way that makes the rest of the cathedral feel like a setting for it.
  • Petřín Hill: A forested hill with a miniature Eiffel Tower observation platform, accessible by funicular from Malá Strana — the view from the top contextualises the entire castle complex.
  • Café Savoy: The restored grand café in Malá Strana is the finest place in Prague for breakfast — vaulted neo-Renaissance ceiling, extraordinary pastries, impeccable coffee.
  • Kutná Hora: An hour from Prague by train, the Sedlec Ossuary — a church decorated with the bones of 40,000 people — is macabre, artistic, and impossible to forget.

Prague is the city that made a careful decision to survive with its beauty intact. Standing in its ancient streets, you understand that this was exactly the right decision.

Photo by Jaromír Kavan on Unsplash

entry.title: Mexico City: Ancient Foundations, Modern Pulse
entry.content:
Mexico City was built on a lake. The Aztec capital of Tenochtitlán rose from the waters of Lake Texcoco on artificial islands connected by causeways, and when the Spanish conquered it in 1521 they built their colonial capital directly on top. The city has been subsiding into its lacustrine foundations ever since — colonial buildings list at angles that would alarm a builder elsewhere — but the layers of civilisation compressed beneath its streets are what make Mexico City one of the most historically dense and culturally extraordinary cities in the Americas.

The Zócalo and Ancient Mexico

The Zócalo — formally the Plaza de la Constitución — is one of the world's great public squares: a vast flat space flanked by the Metropolitan Cathedral (built partly from Aztec temple stones), the National Palace (covered in Diego Rivera murals), and the remains of the Templo Mayor. The Templo Mayor was the ceremonial heart of Tenochtitlán, excavated from beneath modern streets only in 1978 after a worker accidentally struck it with a pickaxe. The adjacent Museo del Templo Mayor displays the extraordinary finds and explains the Aztec cosmology with clarity and depth that few museums achieve.

Roma and Condesa — The Modern City

The neighbourhoods of Roma and Condesa represent Mexico City's contemporary creative life: tree-lined avenues of Art Nouveau and Art Deco buildings converted into excellent restaurants, cafés, bookshops, and galleries. The morning market in the Mercado Medellín is where the neighbourhood cooks shop — the fresh produce, cheese, and flower stalls are extraordinary. The Museo Nacional de Antropología in Chapultepec Park is arguably the finest anthropological museum in the world — the Aztec Sun Stone alone justifies the visit, but the collections spanning all of Mexico's pre-Columbian cultures are overwhelming in their scope and quality.

Gotchas & Tips

  • Altitude Reality: Mexico City sits at 2,240 metres — high enough to cause altitude sickness in some visitors. Drink plenty of water, avoid alcohol the first day, and take the first 24 hours gently regardless of how you feel.
  • The Taco Geography: Mexico City's taco culture is both overwhelming and magnificent. Al pastor from a trompo spit (best in the Condesa area) and consomé de barbacoa on Sunday morning in a traditional market are the two essential experiences. Avoid tourist-oriented taco chains.
  • Traffic and Transport: Mexico City's metro is the second-largest in Latin America, remarkably cheap, and usually the fastest way across the city. The traffic above ground is genuinely challenging. Download the Metro app for navigation.

Highlights

  • Frida Kahlo Museum (La Casa Azul): Kahlo's home in Coyoacán is one of the world's great artistic pilgrimages — vivid, intimate, and genuinely moving. Book tickets weeks in advance.
  • Xochimilco Trajineras: The ancient canal network south of the city, where colourful flat-bottomed boats carry families and musicians through the chinampas (floating gardens) every weekend.
  • Lucha Libre Wrestling: A Friday night match at the Arena México — masks, acrobatics, theatrical villains — is one of the great Mexican cultural spectacles.
  • Palacio de Bellas Artes: The Art Nouveau/Art Deco opera house and cultural centre contains Rivera, Siqueiros, and Orozco murals of staggering quality.

Mexico City does not condescend. It offers everything — history, food, art, chaos, beauty — and trusts you to find your own way through it.

Photo by Dennis Schrader on Unsplash

entry.title: Queenstown: Adventure Capital of the Southern Hemisphere
entry.content:
Queenstown sits in a bowl of mountains that seem designed specifically to accelerate adrenaline. The Remarkables range rises directly from Lake Wakatipu's southern shore in a wall of jagged schist peaks; Coronet Peak commands the northern skyline; and the lake itself — 84 kilometres long, shaped in a Z that local legend explains as the outline of a sleeping giant — reflects everything back with the clarity of perfect mirror water. This is the kind of landscape that makes you want to do something extreme just to feel adequate to it.

The Remarkables and Skyline Gondola

In winter, the Remarkables Ski Area offers one of the most scenic ski fields in the southern hemisphere — the lake visible from almost every run, snow reliable from June through September. In summer, the same terrain becomes mountain biking and hiking territory of remarkable quality. The Skyline Gondola rises 450 metres from the town centre to a ridge where the panoramic view over the lake and surrounding ranges requires a long pause to fully absorb. From the top, the Ben Lomond Track continues another 1,748 metres higher for a full-day summit hike that rewards with views across two distinct mountain ranges.

Glenorchy and the Road to Paradise

The road from Queenstown to Glenorchy — forty-five minutes along the northern shore of Lake Wakatipu — is one of the finest drives in New Zealand, and that is saying something. The mountains press closer, the lake narrows, and the farmland becomes increasingly cinematic (much of the Lord of the Rings landscape was filmed in this area). Beyond Glenorchy, the road continues to Paradise — an aptly named river flat beneath the Dart Glacier — and the start of the Rees-Dart Track, one of New Zealand's great multi-day wilderness walks.

Gotchas & Tips

  • Adrenaline Fatigue is Real: Queenstown's activity operators compete fiercely and the result is excellent safety standards. But with bungee, skydiving, jet boating, white water rafting, and canyon swinging all on offer, choose one or two genuinely meaningful experiences rather than ticking every box.
  • Wine Region Proximity: The Central Otago wine region begins just forty minutes east of Queenstown. Its pinot noir is among the finest in the world — the wineries around Gibbston Valley and Bannockburn offer cellar-door tastings in extraordinary dry schist gorge scenery.
  • Seasonal Timing: Queenstown works year-round but for different reasons. Winter (June to August) is for skiing; summer (December to February) is for hiking and lake activities; autumn (March to May) brings the most spectacular colour — aspens and poplars turning gold against the mountain backdrop.

Highlights

  • Bungee at the Kawarau Bridge: The original commercial bungee jump site from 1988, still spectacular at 43 metres above the river.
  • Fergburger: The legendary Queenstown burger institution — queue at midnight with the après-ski crowd for a burger that justifies every superlative.
  • Lake Wakatipu Steamer: The vintage TSS Earnslaw has been steaming across the lake since 1912, and a round trip to Walter Peak Station remains one of the finest ways to see the mountains from the water.
  • Arrowtown: The historic gold-mining village twenty minutes from Queenstown has the best autumn colour in New Zealand and an excellent museum of the Chinese gold-miners' experience.

Queenstown does not moderate itself. It offers the full volume of the natural world, and the only reasonable response is to say yes.

Photo by Jeff Finley on Unsplash

entry.title: New York: Navigating the Concrete Jungle
entry.content:
New York is a city that doesn't just sleep; it vibrates. As a photographer who thrives on urban energy, NYC is my ultimate playground. Every corner is a frame, every subway ride is a story, and the "concrete jungle" has a beauty that rivals any forest I've ever visited.

Above the Streets

We spent a morning walking The High Line, an elevated park built on a historic freight rail line. It’s a masterclass in urban renewal, weaving between skyscrapers and offering unique "voyeuristic" views into the city's architecture. For lunch, we grabbed supplies and had a Central Park picnic on the Sheep Meadow—the contrast of the green grass against the surrounding Billionaires' Row skyline is quintessentially New York.

To end the day, we skipped the Empire State Building (too crowded!) and went to the Top of the Rock at the Rockefeller Center. Pro tip: this is where you get the best view of the Empire State Building, especially as the lights come on at dusk.

A Slice (and a Bagel) of Heaven

You can't come to New York and not eat your way through the five boroughs. We started our day with a classic everything bagel with lox and a "schmear" of cream cheese from a local deli. It’s the only way to breakfast here. For dinner, we did the "NY shuffle"—standing on the sidewalk eating a $4 slice of pepperoni pizza from Joe’s on Carmine Street. It’s thin, foldable, and exactly what perfection tastes like.

Gotchas & Tips

  • The MetroCard is King: Don't bother with Ubers in Manhattan; the subway is faster and cheaper. Use "OMNY" (tap-to-pay) with your phone to skip the lines at the kiosks.
  • Comfort over Fashion: You will walk 10+ miles a day without realizing it. Wear your best sneakers, not your "fancy" shoes.
  • Look Up: New Yorkers are famous for looking down or straight ahead. If you look up, you’ll see some of the most beautiful Art Deco details in the world.

Highlights

  • The High Line: A peaceful green ribbon in a gray city.
  • Top of the Rock: The best 360-degree view of the city.
  • Joe's Pizza: A culinary landmark that lives up to the hype.
  • Central Park: The "Lungs of the City" and the best place for people-watching.

New York is a city that demands you bring your "A" game. It’s loud, it’s fast, and it’s absolutely intoxicating.

Photo by Luca Bravo on Unsplash

entry.title: Ha Long Bay: Emerald Waters and Limestone Giants
entry.content:
The karst limestone islands of Ha Long Bay rise from jade-green water in shapes that seem designed rather than formed — pinnacles, arches, caves, and towers that local legend attributes to a dragon descending from the heavens to protect Vietnam from invaders. There are nearly two thousand islands in the bay, most uninhabited, covered in subtropical jungle that reaches almost to the waterline. Travelling through them by boat — which is the only real way — creates a sustained sense of passage through a landscape that the human mind is not quite equipped to process.

Cruising the Bay

Ha Long Bay is best experienced on a two or three-night cruise aboard a traditional junk boat. Budget options travel the more congested southern zones; premium operators navigate the UNESCO-listed core zone and the quieter Cat Ba Island area. The rhythm of life on board — slow breakfasts on deck, kayaking into flooded cave systems, swimming from the boat as the sun drops behind the limestone — is genuinely one of the finest ways to travel anywhere in Southeast Asia. Lan Ha Bay, adjacent to Ha Long but falling under Cat Ba Island's jurisdiction, sees a fraction of the visitor numbers for a nearly identical landscape.

Caves, Kayaks, and Fishing Villages

The Hang Sung Sot (Surprising Cave) is the largest cave in the bay and lives up to its name — cathedral-scale chambers lit by coloured lights that are more dramatic than they sound. Better, because more intimate, is kayaking through a narrow sea arch into a hidden lagoon, surrounded on all sides by vertical limestone and absolute silence. The floating fishing villages that still exist within the bay — communities living year-round on houseboats — are slowly being relocated to shore, making the handful that remain worth visiting with a responsible guide while they still exist.

Gotchas & Tips

  • Boat Quality Varies Enormously: The difference between a cheap overnight boat and a mid-range cruise is significant in terms of safety, hygiene, and experience. Read recent reviews carefully and choose an operator certified by the Vietnam National Administration of Tourism.
  • Weather Seasonality: Ha Long Bay is best visited October to April. May to September brings typhoon season risk and heavy rain. The winter months (December to February) can be cool and misty — many find the fog adds to the atmosphere; others find it frustrating for visibility.
  • The Hanoi Connection: Ha Long Bay is a four-hour bus journey from Hanoi, or a seaplane for those with less time. Most cruise operators include transport in the package price. Spending at least two nights in Hanoi before or after is strongly recommended.

Highlights

  • Sunrise from the Boat Deck: The early morning light over the limestone islands, before other boats are moving, is the bay at its most serene and extraordinary.
  • Kayaking into Ti Top Island Lagoon: The small enclosed bay at Ti Top Island, accessible only by kayak through a low arch, offers a private moment of near-total isolation.
  • Squid Fishing at Night: Many cruise operators set up squid fishing off the stern deck after dark. The bioluminescent plankton in the disturbed water around the lights is an unexpected spectacle.
  • Cat Ba Town: The main settlement on Cat Ba Island has a genuine Vietnamese fishing town character, with excellent seafood restaurants and access to Cat Ba National Park hiking.

Ha Long Bay asks only that you slow down enough to look. The landscape will take care of the rest.

Photo by Long Nguyễn on Unsplash

entry.title: Amalfi Coast: Winding Roads and Salty Air
entry.content:
The Amalfi Coast is a vertical landscape where colorful houses cling to the cliffs like brightly colored barnacles. Being a bit of a history geek, I was less interested in the luxury beach clubs and more fascinated by the fact that this rugged coastline was once one of the most powerful maritime republics in the Mediterranean.

Driving the Dream (and the Nightmare)

There is nothing quite like driving the SS163, the "Road of a Thousand Bends." With the scent of lemons blowing through the window and the salty Mediterranean air, it’s pure bliss—if you don't mind the white-knuckle adrenaline of a tour bus coming at you on a hairpin turn!

For a change of pace, we hiked the Path of the Gods (Sentiero degli Dei). This trail high above the sea offers views that genuinely made me stop and catch my breath. We ended our day with a private Positano boat tour, looking back at the pyramid of pastel houses as the sun dipped below the horizon. Seeing Positano from the water is the only way to truly understand its scale.

A Seafood Symphony

Dinner in Amalfi usually starts and ends with lemons. We sat at a tiny trattoria tucked away from the main piazza and had Scialatielli ai frutti di mare—thick, hand-rolled pasta served with a bounty of clams, mussels, and shrimp. And of course, no meal is complete without a chilled glass of local Limoncello. It’s liquid sunshine!

Gotchas & Tips

  • Ditch the Car: Unless you have nerves of steel, take the SITA bus or the ferry. Parking is nearly non-existent and incredibly expensive.
  • The "Steps" Tax: Be prepared for steps. Thousands of them. If you have mobility issues, stay in Amalfi or Maiori rather than Positano.
  • Reservations are King: If you want a table with a view for sunset, book at least 2-3 days in advance during the summer months.

The Amalfi Coast is a place of dramatic beauty and deep history. It’s a bit crowded, yes, but some things are famous for a reason.

Highlights

  • Path of the Gods: The best free view in Italy.
  • Positano from the water: Pure cinematic magic.
  • Scialatielli: The texture of the pasta is unforgettable.
  • Amalfi Cathedral: A stunning blend of Arab-Norman architecture.

Stay tuned for more updates from our Italian summer!

Photo by Tom Podmore on Unsplash

entry.title: Santorini: The Blue and White Dream
entry.content:
As a photographer, Santorini is both my greatest dream and my hardest challenge. How do you capture the contrast of those impossible blue domes against a sea that seems even bluer? It’s a place where the light is so crisp it feels like you could reach out and snap off a piece of it.

The Caldera Hike

We avoided the tourist donkeys and took the legendary 10km hike from Fira to Oia. It’s rugged, dusty, and offers the most breathtaking caldera views on the island. We timed it so we arrived in Oia just as the golden hour began. While the main streets were packed, we found a quiet spot near the Byzantine Castle ruins to watch the sun dip into the Aegean. It’s a cliché for a reason—the sky turns colors I didn't know existed.

We also took a boat tour to the Nea Kameni volcano. Walking on the dark, volcanic rock and then swimming in the warm, orange-tinted Palea Kameni hot springs is the perfect counterpoint to the pristine white villages above.

A Taste of the Volcanic Soil

The volcanic soil of Santorini produces some of the most flavorful vegetables I've ever tasted. We spent an afternoon at a local taverna in Pyrgos where I fell in love with Fava—a creamy yellow split pea purée topped with capers and red onion. But the real star was the Tomatokeftedes (tomato fritters). Crispy on the outside, bursting with the juice of sun-ripened cherry tomatoes on the inside.

Gotchas & Tips

  • The Cruise Ship Wave: If you're staying on the island, find out when the cruise ships are docked. Use those hours to explore the inland villages like Emporio or Pyrgos instead of Fira/Oia.
  • The Sun is Real: There is very little shade on the Fira-Oia hike. Wear a hat and start before 8 AM.
  • Akrotiri is a Gem: Don't just stay on the surface. The prehistoric ruins of Akrotiri (the "Greek Pompeii") are preserved in such detail it’s mind-blowing.

Highlights

  • Fira to Oia Hike: 10km of pure coastal drama.
  • Byzantine Castle Sunset: The most famous sunset in the world for a reason.
  • Akrotiri: A fascinating look into a Bronze Age city.
  • Tomato Fritters: The best snack you’ll find in the Cyclades.

Santorini is a place of fire and light. It’s an island that demands you put down your phone and just stare at the horizon for a while.
